source.title: Validity of the Wattbike 3-Minute Aerobic Test: Measurement and Estimation of V̇o2max

paper.citation: Hanson N.J., Scheadler C.M., Katsavelis D., Miller M.G. Validity of the Wattbike 3-Minute Aerobic Test: Measurement and Estimation of V̇o2max. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2022;36(2):400-404. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000003440.
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Does the Wattbike three-minute aerobic test elicit a measured V̇O2max comparable with a self-paced maximal test, and does the Wattbike software estimate agree with the measured criterion? Thirteen low-risk adults with recent cycling experience completed the study: ten men and three women, mean age 29.2 years, with widely varying cycling histories. Participants were recruited from a university and local cycling clubs and averaged approximately 107 km of cycling per week. This was a repeated-measures validation study across two visits. Participants first completed a 10-minute self-paced maximal oxygen-uptake test, then 48 hours to one week later completed the Wattbike three-minute aerobic test after a standardized 20-minute warm-up.
paper.tldr: Mean estimated V̇O2max from the Wattbike, measured V̇O2max during the three-minute test, and measured V̇O2max during the self-paced criterion test did not differ statistically. The correlation between measured V̇O2max in the self-paced and three-minute tests was high at ICC 0.96, and the association between the self-paced measure and Wattbike estimate was also high at ICC 0.91. The Wattbike three-minute test can be a pragmatic estimate when cycle testing is appropriate, athletes complete the full warm-up, and the same protocol is standardized over time.
paper.methods: This was a repeated-measures validation study across two visits. Participants first completed a 10-minute self-paced maximal oxygen-uptake test, then 48 hours to one week later completed the Wattbike three-minute aerobic test after a standardized 20-minute warm-up. A metabolic cart measured respiratory variables in both sessions, and the Wattbike supplied its proprietary estimate. Repeated-measures comparisons, intraclass correlations, and Bland-Altman agreement analyses were used.
paper.findings: Mean estimated V̇O2max from the Wattbike, measured V̇O2max during the three-minute test, and measured V̇O2max during the self-paced criterion test did not differ statistically. The correlation between measured V̇O2max in the self-paced and three-minute tests was high at ICC 0.96, and the association between the self-paced measure and Wattbike estimate was also high at ICC 0.91. Mean bias between the Wattbike estimate and self-paced measured V̇O2max was only 0.29 mL per kg per minute, but individual 95% limits of agreement were wide, approximately minus 10.77 to plus 11.34 mL per kg per minute. The three-minute test produced higher carbon-dioxide output and respiratory exchange ratio and a slightly lower peak heart rate than the self-paced test, indicating that the protocols were physiologically similar in V̇O2max but not interchangeable in all responses. Eight participants used a conservative or even-paced strategy and five used an aggressive declining-power strategy; both patterns reached similar maximal oxygen uptake in this small sample. The standardized 20-minute warm-up likely contributed to successful V̇O2max attainment and is part of the tested protocol rather than an optional detail.
paper.limitations: The validation sample was only 13 cyclists, included just three women, and spanned broad age and training experience. Test order was fixed rather than randomized, the self-paced test was treated as the criterion rather than compared against a conventional graded test in the same study, and the proprietary estimation equation was not recalibrated or externally cross-validated. High correlation and similar group means do not guarantee close individual agreement, as shown by limits spanning roughly 22 mL per kg per minute. The study assessed concurrent validity, not test-retest reliability or sensitivity to training change. Direct applicability to collegiate American football is limited because cyclists were tested in a cycling-specific modality and V̇O2max is not a complete measure of football conditioning.
paper.practicalImplications: The Wattbike three-minute test can be a pragmatic estimate when cycle testing is appropriate, athletes complete the full warm-up, and the same protocol is standardized over time. Use the result for broad profiling or within-athlete trends, not as a precise laboratory-equivalent number for an individual. Before adopting it with collegiate American football players, establish familiarization, repeatability, positional tolerability, and local comparison with the program’s reference conditioning measures. Account for the test’s high anaerobic demand and avoid testing when fatigue or lower-limb status makes a maximal three-minute effort inappropriate.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete development, the Wattbike three-minute test can be a pragmatic estimate when cycle testing is appropriate, athletes complete the full warm-up, and the same protocol is standardized over time. Before adopting it with collegiate American football players, establish familiarization, repeatability, positional tolerability, and local comparison with the program’s reference conditioning measures. paper.rtp: The paper did not validate a rehabilitation or return-to-sport decision rule. Its findings may inform supporting training or monitoring during reconditioning, but it provides no standalone clearance threshold or progression criterion.
